title: Who May Dwell on Your Holy Mountain?
summary: The psalm asks who may live in the LORD's tent and dwell on his holy mountain. The answer is a portrait of a person of integrity: truthful in heart, harmless to neighbors, loyal to those who fear God, faithful to oaths even when costly, honest with money, and incorruptible in court. Such a person will never be shaken.
story: Psalm 14 ended with God looking down and finding no one who does good, followed by a longing for salvation from Zion. Psalm 15 asks the natural next question: who, then, may come into God's presence on Zion? The answer does not list rituals or sacrifices but everyday conduct: speech, friendship, money, promises, and justice. Scholars have noticed that Psalms 15 to 24 seem to be arranged in a mirror pattern, with Psalm 15 and Psalm 24 (another psalm about who may ascend the LORD's hill) as matching bookends and Psalm 19, the great psalm of creation and Torah, at the center. Whether or not that pattern was intended, the Psalter is clearly placing ethics at the gate of worship.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David. The picture of God's tent on his holy mountain fits the period after David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem and placed it in a tent he had pitched for it (2 Samuel 6:17), before Solomon built the temple. Scholars who date the psalm later note that tent language remained part of Israel's poetry for the temple long after the tabernacle itself was gone, so the imagery doesn't fix the date.

Many scholars classify Psalm 15 as an entrance liturgy, a form of worship used at the sanctuary gate. Pilgrims arriving for a festival may have asked the question of verse 1, and a priest or Levite answered with the conditions of verse 2 to 5. Psalm 24:3-6 and Isaiah 33:14-16 have a similar question-and-answer shape. Other scholars think the psalm is a teaching poem modeled on that form rather than a script for a gate ceremony.
cultural:
The tent and the holy mountain point to the tabernacle and to Zion in Jerusalem. To sojourn (the verb of verse 1, rendered “abide”) was to live as a guest under someone's protection, and ancient Near Eastern hospitality laid heavy obligations on both host and guest. The question is what kind of guest may live in God's household.

Several of the conditions reflect Israel's laws. The ban on lending money at interest to a fellow Israelite comes from Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:35-37, and Deuteronomy 23:19-20. In an agricultural economy, loans were usually made to neighbors in distress after a bad harvest, and interest could push a family into debt slavery and the loss of its land. The refusal of bribes echoes Exodus 23:8 and Deuteronomy 16:19, which warn that a bribe blinds the eyes of judges. Keeping an oath even when it proves costly reflects the seriousness of vows made before God (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). The Babylonian Talmud, in the tractate Makkot, records a rabbinic tradition that David summed up the commandments of the Torah in the eleven qualities of this psalm.
literary: The psalm has a question-and-answer structure framed by a promise. Verse 1 asks two parallel questions. Verses 2 to 5a answer with a series of qualities, moving from positive statements (walks with integrity, practices righteousness, speaks truth) to negative ones (no slander, no harm, no scorn) and back through a mix of social, legal, and financial conduct. Verse 5b closes with a promise that turns the question around: the one who does these things will never be shaken. The verbs of verse 1 (abide, dwell) are matched by the verb of the last line (be shaken), so that the psalm moves from entering God's presence to stability in it.

outline.t: Heading and the question: who may dwell with the LORD?
Integrity in heart, word, and relationships
Honest money, incorruptible justice, and an unshaken life

doctrines.note: To live near a holy God requires a life that reflects his character. The psalm defines holiness not through ritual but through truthfulness, justice, and faithfulness to neighbors.
The conditions of the psalm summarize the ethical heart of Israel's law, including the laws on lending, bribery, and oaths. The law's purpose is life in God's presence.

Much of the psalm concerns the neighbor and the friend: no harm, no slander, no scorn. God's covenant binds his people to him and to one another, so life with God is inseparable from how one treats the community around him.

words.note: Gur, to sojourn or abide as a guest. The verb describes a resident outsider who lives under a host's protection, like Abraham in Canaan. To ask who may sojourn in God's tent is to ask who may be welcomed into his household as a guest, which implies that no one lives there by natural right.

Tamim, blameless or whole. The word describes a sacrificial animal without defect and a person whose life is complete and undivided in devotion to God (Genesis 6:9; Genesis 17:1). In verse 2 it means integrity, a consistency between inner character and outward conduct, not sinless perfection.

Neshek, interest. The word literally means a bite, a vivid picture of how interest could consume a struggling borrower. Israel's law forbade charging it to fellow Israelites in need. The psalm counts this financial decision as part of what it means to dwell with God.

Mot, to shake or totter. The verb is used of a mountain or a foundation moving. The promise that the one who lives this way will never be shaken echoes the stability of God's holy mountain itself, and it contrasts with the wicked man of Psalm 10:6, who boasts that he will not be moved.

christ: Psalm 15 sets a standard no one fully meets, a point Psalm 14 has just made. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who perfectly walked with integrity, spoke truth from his heart, and did no harm to his neighbor. Hebrews says believers have confidence to enter the holy places by his blood (Hebrews 10:19). Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount takes up the same concerns: truthful speech and a simple yes or no in place of manipulative oaths (Matthew 5:33-37), and generosity in lending without expecting return (Luke 6:35). The link is both ethical and redemptive: Christ is the one who fits the psalm's portrait, and through him others are welcomed onto God's holy mountain and shaped into that likeness.

hard.q: Does this psalm teach that we earn access to God by good behavior?
hard.a: Read alone, Psalm 15 could sound like a list of requirements for admission. But in Israel's worship, access to God was always grounded first in his covenant grace; the law was given to a people already rescued from Egypt. The psalm describes the character of those who belong in God's presence, not a fee paid at the door. Christians read it in two ways at once. It exposes that none of us fully meets the standard (as Psalm 14 and Romans 3 insist), which drives us to the grace of God in Christ. And it describes the kind of life that grace produces, since those welcomed into God's household are meant to become like its host.

questions: Which of the qualities in verses 2 to 5 comes most naturally to you, and which is hardest?
The psalm links worship with how we handle money, promises, and speech. What would change if your church took that link seriously?
Verse 4 praises someone who keeps a costly promise. When has keeping your word cost you something, and what did you learn?
